claim: During transcription initiation, RNA polymerase (RNAP) binds to promoter DNA, unwinds promoter DNA to form an RNAP-promoter open complex (RPo) containing a single-stranded 'transcription bubble,' and selects a transcription start site (TSS).
source: During transcription initiation, RNA polymerase (RNAP) binds to promoter DNA, unwinds promoter DNA to form an RNAP-promoter open complex (RPo) containing a single-stranded 'transcription bubble,' and selects a transcription start site (TSS).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the transcription initiation process.

claim: TSS selection occurs at different positions within the promoter region, depending on promoter sequence and initiating-substrate concentration.
source: TSS selection occurs at different positions within the promoter region, depending on promoter sequence and initiating-substrate concentration.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations in the manuscript.

claim: Variability in TSS selection has been proposed to involve DNA 'scrunching' and 'anti-scrunching,' the hallmarks of which are: (i) forward and reverse movement of the RNAP leading edge, but not trailing edge, relative to DNA, and (ii) expansion and contraction of the transcription bubble.
source: Variability in TSS selection has been proposed to involve DNA 'scrunching' and 'anti-scrunching,' the hallmarks of which are: (i) forward and reverse movement of the RNAP leading edge, but not trailing edge, relative to DNA, and (ii) expansion and contraction of the transcription bubble.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior work that the current study tests.

claim: Bacterial TSS selection exhibits both hallmarks of scrunching and anti-scrunching in vitro and in vivo.
source: Here, using in vitro and in vivo protein-DNA photocrosslinking and single-molecule nanomanipulation, we show bacterial TSS selection exhibits both hallmarks of scrunching and anti-scrunching, and we define energetics of scrunching and anti-scrunching.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data from protein-DNA photocrosslinking and single-molecule nanomanipulation experiments.

claim: The energetics of scrunching and anti-scrunching in bacterial TSS selection have been defined.
source: Here, using in vitro and in vivo protein-DNA photocrosslinking and single-molecule nanomanipulation, we show bacterial TSS selection exhibits both hallmarks of scrunching and anti-scrunching, and we define energetics of scrunching and anti-scrunching.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from single-molecule nanomanipulation experiments measuring primer-concentration dependences.

claim: The results establish the mechanism of TSS selection by bacterial RNAP.
source: The results establish the mechanism of TSS selection by bacterial RNAP and suggest a general mechanism for TSS selection by bacterial, archaeal, and eukaryotic RNAP.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: The mechanism of TSS selection by bacterial RNAP suggests a general mechanism for TSS selection by bacterial, archaeal, and eukaryotic RNAP.
source: The results establish the mechanism of TSS selection by bacterial RNAP and suggest a general mechanism for TSS selection by bacterial, archaeal, and eukaryotic RNAP.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the bacterial RNAP data and knowledge of similarities across RNAP systems.

claim: TSS selection by bacterial RNAP involves four promoter-sequence determinants: distance relative to the promoter −10 element, identities of template-strand nucleotides at and upstream of the TSS, the promoter core recognition element, and the promoter discriminator element.
source: TSS selection by bacterial RNAP and the bacterial transcription initiation factor σ involves four promoter-sequence determinants: (i) distance relative to the promoter −10 element (preference for TSS selection at the position 7 bp downstream of the promoter −10 element; Aoyama and Takanami, 1985; Sørensen et al., 1993; Jeong and Kang, 1994; Liu and Turnbough, 1994; Walker and Osuna, 2002; Lewis and Adhya, 2004; Vvedenskaya et al., 2015; Winkelman et al., 2016a; Winkelman et al., 2016b); (ii) identities of the template-strand nucleotide at the TSS and the template-strand nucleotide immediately upstream of the TSS (strong preference for a template-strand pyrimidine at the TSS and preference for a template-strand purine immediately upstream of the TSS; Aoyama and Takanami, 1985; Sørensen et al., 1993; Jeong and Kang, 1994; Liu and Turnbough, 1994; Walker and Osuna, 2002; Lewis and Adhya, 2004; Vvedenskaya et al., 2015; Winkelman et al., 2016a; Winkelman et al., 2016b); (iii) the promoter 'core recognition element,' a segment of nontemplate-strand sequence spanning the TSS that interacts sequence-specifically with RNAP (preference for nontemplate-strand G immediately downstream of the TSS; Vvedenskaya et al., 2016), and (iv) the promoter 'discriminator element,' a nontemplate-strand sequence immediately downstream of the promoter −10 element that interacts sequence-specifically with σ (preference for TSS selection at upstream positions for purine-rich discriminator sequences, and preference for TSS selection at downstream positions for pyrimidine-rich discriminator sequences; Winkelman et al., 2016a, 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: There is a preference for TSS selection at the position 7 bp downstream of the promoter −10 element.
source: distance relative to the promoter −10 element (preference for TSS selection at the position 7 bp downstream of the promoter −10 element; Aoyama and Takanami, 1985; Sørensen et al., 1993; Jeong and Kang, 1994; Liu and Turnbough, 1994; Walker and Osuna, 2002; Lewis and Adhya, 2004; Vvedenskaya et al., 2015; Winkelman et al., 2016a; Winkelman et al., 2016b)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: There is a strong preference for a template-strand pyrimidine at the TSS and preference for a template-strand purine immediately upstream of the TSS.
source: identities of the template-strand nucleotide at the TSS and the template-strand nucleotide immediately upstream of the TSS (strong preference for a template-strand pyrimidine at the TSS and preference for a template-strand purine immediately upstream of the TSS; Aoyama and Takanami, 1985; Sørensen et al., 1993; Jeong and Kang, 1994; Liu and Turnbough, 1994; Walker and Osuna, 2002; Lewis and Adhya, 2004; Vvedenskaya et al., 2015; Winkelman et al., 2016a; Winkelman et al., 2016b)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The promoter core recognition element shows preference for nontemplate-strand G immediately downstream of the TSS.
source: the promoter 'core recognition element,' a segment of nontemplate-strand sequence spanning the TSS that interacts sequence-specifically with RNAP (preference for nontemplate-strand G immediately downstream of the TSS; Vvedenskaya et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The promoter discriminator element shows preference for TSS selection at upstream positions for purine-rich discriminator sequences, and preference for TSS selection at downstream positions for pyrimidine-rich discriminator sequences.
source: the promoter 'discriminator element,' a nontemplate-strand sequence immediately downstream of the promoter −10 element that interacts sequence-specifically with σ (preference for TSS selection at upstream positions for purine-rich discriminator sequences, and preference for TSS selection at downstream positions for pyrimidine-rich discriminator sequences; Winkelman et al., 2016a, 2016b)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The concentrations of initiating NTPs influence TSS selection.
source: In addition to these four promoter-sequence determinants, the concentrations of initiating NTPs (Sørensen et al., 1993; Liu and Turnbough, 1994; Walker and Osuna, 2002; Vvedenskaya et al., 2015; Wilson et al., 1992; Qi and Turnbough, 1995; Tu and Turnbough, 1997; Walker et al., 2004; Turnbough, 2008; Turnbough and Switzer, 2008) and DNA topology (Vvedenskaya et al., 2015) also influence TSS selection.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: DNA topology influences TSS selection.
source: In addition to these four promoter-sequence determinants, the concentrations of initiating NTPs (Sørensen et al., 1993; Liu and Turnbough, 1994; Walker and Osuna, 2002; Vvedenskaya et al., 2015; Wilson et al., 1992; Qi and Turnbough, 1995; Tu and Turnbough, 1997; Walker et al., 2004; Turnbough, 2008; Turnbough and Switzer, 2008) and DNA topology (Vvedenskaya et al., 2015) also influence TSS selection.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In previous work, TSS selection was shown to exhibit the first hallmark of scrunching in vitro.
source: In previous work, we showed that TSS selection exhibits the first hallmark of scrunching in vitro (Winkelman et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is a reference to prior work by the authors.

claim: Replacing a GGG discriminator by a CCT discriminator causes a 2 bp downstream change in TSS from position 7 bp to position 9 bp downstream of the −10 element.
source: For example, replacing a GGG discriminator by a CCT discriminator causes a 2 bp downstream change in TSS (from the position 7 bp downstream of the −10 element to the position 9 bp downstream of the −10 element, due to differences in sequence-specific σ-DNA interaction that result in different paths of the DNA nontemplate strand), causes a 2 bp downstream change in RNAP leading-edge position, but does not cause a change in RNAP trailing-edge position (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Replacing a GGG discriminator by a CCT discriminator causes a 2 bp downstream change in RNAP leading-edge position but does not cause a change in RNAP trailing-edge position.
source: For example, replacing a GGG discriminator by a CCT discriminator causes a 2 bp downstream change in TSS (from the position 7 bp downstream of the −10 element to the position 9 bp downstream of the −10 element, due to differences in sequence-specific σ-DNA interaction that result in different paths of the DNA nontemplate strand), causes a 2 bp downstream change in RNAP leading-edge position, but does not cause a change in RNAP trailing-edge position (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The discriminator element influences TSS selection through effects on sequence-specific σ-DNA interaction that select between two alternative paths of the DNA nontemplate strand.
source: The results showed that the discriminator element (Haugen et al., 2006; Feklistov et al., 2006) influences TSS selection and does so through effects on sequence-specific σ-DNA interaction that select between two alternative paths of the DNA nontemplate strand (Winkelman et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: There is an exact correspondence of crosslinking patterns in vitro and in vivo for TSS selection.
source: The results showed an exact correspondence of crosslinking patterns in vitro and in vivo (Figure 1B, 'in vitro' vs. 'in vivo' lanes).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B comparing in vitro and in vivo results.

claim: The RNAP leading edge crosslinked 2 bp further downstream on CCT than on GGG, whereas the RNAP trailing edge crosslinked at the same positions on CCT and GGG.
source: The RNAP leading edge crosslinked 2 bp further downstream on CCT than on GGG, whereas the RNAP trailing edge crosslinked at the same positions on CCT and GGG (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: TSS selection in vivo shows the first hallmark of scrunching.
source: We conclude that TSS selection in vivo shows the first hallmark of scrunching.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vivo crosslinking data.

claim: Transition amplitudes for RNAP-dependent DNA unwinding upon formation of RPo with CCT are larger than those for formation of RPo with GGG, on both positively and negatively supercoiled templates.
source: The results indicate that transition amplitudes for RNAP-dependent DNA unwinding upon formation of RPo with CCT are larger than those for formation of RPo with GGG, on both positively and negatively supercoiled templates (Figure 2B, left and center).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There is a 2 bp difference in RNAP-dependent DNA unwinding for CCT vs. GGG.
source: By combining the results with positively and negatively supercoiled templates to deconvolve effects of RNAP-dependent DNA unwinding and RNAP-dependent compaction (Revyakin et al., 2004, 2005, 2006), we find a 2 bp difference in RNAP-dependent DNA unwinding for CCT vs. GGG (Figure 2C), corresponding exactly to the 2 bp difference in TSS selection (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and comparison to Figure 1B.

claim: The 2 bp difference in RNAP-dependent DNA unwinding for CCT vs. GGG corresponds exactly to the 2 bp difference in TSS selection.
source: By combining the results with positively and negatively supercoiled templates to deconvolve effects of RNAP-dependent DNA unwinding and RNAP-dependent compaction (Revyakin et al., 2004, 2005, 2006), we find a 2 bp difference in RNAP-dependent DNA unwinding for CCT vs. GGG (Figure 2C), corresponding exactly to the 2 bp difference in TSS selection (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of experimental data from Figures 1B and 2C.

claim: TSS selection shows the second hallmark of scrunching.
source: We conclude that TSS selection shows the second hallmark of scrunching.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the DNA nanomanipulation data showing changes in transcription bubble size.

claim: According to the scrunching/anti-scrunching hypothesis, TSS selection at the modal TSS position involves neither scrunching nor anti-scrunching, TSS selection downstream of the modal position involves scrunching, and TSS selection upstream of the modal position involves anti-scrunching.
source: According to the hypothesis that TSS selection involves scrunching or anti-scrunching, TSS selection at the most frequently observed, modal TSS position (7 bp downstream of −10 element for majority of discriminator sequences, including GGG) involves neither scrunching nor anti-scrunching, TSS selection downstream of the modal position involves scrunching (transcription-bubble expansion), and TSS selection upstream of the modal position involves anti-scrunching (Vvedenskaya et al., 2015; Winkelman et al., 2016a, 2016b; Vvedenskaya et al., 2016; Robb et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior work cited in the manuscript.

claim: Successive single-base-pair changes in TSS selection are matched by successive single-base-pair changes in RNAP leading-edge position.
source: The results show that successive single-base-pair changes in TSS selection are matched by successive single-base-pair changes in RNAP leading-edge position.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the primer-programmed TSS selection experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: The first hallmark of scrunching is observed for a full range of TSS positions, including a position upstream of the modal TSS expected to involve anti-scrunching.
source: We conclude that the first hallmark of scrunching is observed for a full range of TSS positions, including, importantly, a position upstream of the modal TSS expected to involve anti-scrunching.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the primer-programmed TSS selection experiments.

claim: With primer GGA, which programs TSS selection at the modal position, DNA unwinding was exactly as in experiments with no primer.
source: With primer GGA, which programs TSS selection at the modal position (7 bp downstream of the −10 element for this discriminator sequence), DNA unwinding was exactly as in experiments with no primer (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: With primers GAA and AAU, which program TSS selection 1 and 2 bp further downstream, DNA unwinding was ~1 and ~2 bp greater than with GGA.
source: With primers GAA and AAU, which program TSS selection 1 and 2 bp further downstream (positions 8 and 9), DNA unwinding was ~1 and ~2 bp greater than with GGA (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: With primer UGG, which programs TSS selection 1 bp upstream, DNA unwinding was ~1 bp less than that in experiments with GGA.
source: With primer UGG, which programs TSS selection 1 bp upstream, DNA unwinding was ~1 bp less than that in experiments with GGA (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Successive single-base-pair changes in TSS selection are matched by successive single-base-pair changes in DNA unwinding for a full range of TSS positions including a position upstream of the modal TSS expected to involve anti-scrunching.
source: The results show that successive single-base-pair changes in TSS selection are matched by successive single-base-pair changes in DNA unwinding for a full range of TSS positions including, importantly, a position upstream of the modal TSS expected to involve anti-scrunching.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the primer-programmed TSS selection experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: The results of protein-DNA photocrosslinking and DNA-nanomanipulation demonstrate, definitively, the scrunching/anti-scrunching hypothesis for TSS selection.
source: Taken together, the results of protein-DNA photocrosslinking (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and DNA-nanomanipulation (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 2) demonstrate, definitively, the scrunching/anti-scrunching hypothesis for TSS selection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental data.

claim: For each primer, increasing the primer concentration increases the lifetime of the unwound state.
source: For each primer, increasing the primer concentration increases the lifetime of the unwound state (tunwound), as expected for coupled equilibria of promoter unwinding, promoter scrunching, and primer binding (Figures 5–6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5-6.

claim: Scrunching by 1 bp requires 0.7 kcal/mol.
source: The results indicate that scrunching by 1 bp requires 0.7 kcal/mol, scrunching by 2 bp requires 1.7 kcal/mol, and anti-scrunching by 1 bp requires 1.8 kcal/mol (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and calculations shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Scrunching by 2 bp requires 1.7 kcal/mol.
source: The results indicate that scrunching by 1 bp requires 0.7 kcal/mol, scrunching by 2 bp requires 1.7 kcal/mol, and anti-scrunching by 1 bp requires 1.8 kcal/mol (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and calculations shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Anti-scrunching by 1 bp requires 1.8 kcal/mol.
source: The results indicate that scrunching by 1 bp requires 0.7 kcal/mol, scrunching by 2 bp requires 1.7 kcal/mol, and anti-scrunching by 1 bp requires 1.8 kcal/mol (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and calculations shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The results provide the first experimental determination of the energetic costs of scrunching and anti-scrunching in any context.
source: The results provide the first experimental determination of the energetic costs of scrunching and anti-scrunching in any context.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: Energetic costs on the scale of ~0.7–1.8 kcal/mol per scrunched bp also apply in the structurally and mechanistically related scrunching that occurs during initial transcription by RNAP.
source: We hypothesize that energetic costs on the same scale, ~0.7–1.8 kcal/mol per scrunched bp, also apply in the structurally and mechanistically related scrunching that occurs during initial transcription by RNAP (Revyakin et al., 2006; Kapanidis et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a hypothesis extrapolating from the current findings to a related process.

claim: The scrunching by ~10 bp that occurs during initial transcription results in an increase in the state energy of the transcription initiation complex by a total of ~7–18 kcal/mol.
source: We note that, according to this hypothesis, the scrunching by ~10 bp that occurs during initial transcription (Revyakin et al., 2006) results in an increase in the state energy of the transcription initiation complex by a total of ~7–18 kcal/mol (~10 x ~0.7–1.8 kcal/mol).
evidence: This is a calculation based on the hypothesis about energetic costs per bp.

claim: The increase in state energy from scrunching during initial transcription is potentially sufficient to yield a 'stressed intermediate' having scrunching-dependent 'stress' comparable to the free energies of RNAP-promoter and RNAP-initiation-factor interactions.
source: This is an increase in state energy potentially sufficient to yield a 'stressed intermediate' (Revyakin et al., 2006; Straney and Crothers, 1987) having scrunching-dependent 'stress' comparable to the free energies of RNAP-promoter and RNAP-initiation-factor interactions that anchor RNAP at a promoter (~7–9 kcal/mol for sequence-specific component of RNAP-promoter interaction and ~13 kcal/mol for RNAP-initiation-factor interaction; 24) and therefore is an increase in state energy potentially sufficient to pay energetic costs of breaking RNAP-promoter and RNAP-initiation-factor interactions in the transition from transcription initiation to transcription elongation.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the functional significance of the energetic costs.

claim: The ΔGscrunch values for bacterial TSS selection account for the range of TSS positions and the relative utilization of different TSS positions in bacterial transcription initiation.
source: The ΔGscrunch values for bacterial TSS selection obtained in this work account for the range of TSS positions and the relative utilization of different TSS positions in bacterial transcription initiation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the energetic data and comparison to observed TSS distributions.

claim: The ΔGscrunch values for TSS selection at positions 6, 7, 8, and 9 of a promoter where the modal TSS is position 7 are all less than or comparable to 3kBT (~2 kcal/mol).
source: The ΔGscrunch values for TSS selection at positions 6, 7, 8, and 9 of a promoter where the modal TSS is position 7 (0–1.8 kcal/mol) all are less than or comparable to 3kBT (~2 kcal/mol), where kB is the Bolztmann constant and T is temperature in °K, indicating that TSS selection at these positions requires no energy beyond energy available in the thermal bath.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the energetic data.

claim: TSS selection at positions 6, 7, 8, and 9 requires no energy beyond energy available in the thermal bath.
source: The ΔGscrunch values for TSS selection at positions 6, 7, 8, and 9 of a promoter where the modal TSS is position 7 (0–1.8 kcal/mol) all are less than or comparable to 3kBT (~2 kcal/mol), where kB is the Bolztmann constant and T is temperature in °K, indicating that TSS selection at these positions requires no energy beyond energy available in the thermal bath.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the energetic data.

claim: The probabilities of TSS selection at positions 6, 7, 8, and 9 as observed in a comprehensive analysis of TSS-region sequences (8%, 55%, 29%, 7%) can be predicted from the Boltzmann-distribution probabilities for the ΔGscrunch values for TSS selection at these positions (3%, 70%, 23%, 4%).
source: Indeed, the probabilities of TSS selection at positions 6, 7, 8, and 9 as observed in a comprehensive analysis of TSS-region sequences (8%, 55%, 29%, 7%; Vvedenskaya et al., 2015) can be predicted from the Boltzmann-distribution probabilities for the ΔGscrunch values for TSS selection at these positions (3%, 70%, 23%, 4%; Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of predicted and observed TSS distributions shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Values of ΔGscrunch for scrunching and anti-scrunching in TSS selection are ~1 kcal mol−1 bp−1 and ~2 kcal mol−1 bp−1, respectively.
source: The finding that values of ΔGscrunch for scrunching and anti-scrunching in TSS selection are ~1 kcal mol−1 bp−1 and ~2 kcal mol−1 bp−1, respectively, implies that TSS selection at positions >2 bp downstream or >1 bp upstream of the modal position would exceed the energy fluctuations available to 99% of molecules at 20–37°C, and therefore explains the observation that TSS selection >2 bp downstream or >1 bp upstream of the modal position occurs rarely (Vvedenskaya et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the energetic data.

claim: TSS selection at positions >2 bp downstream or >1 bp upstream of the modal position would exceed the energy fluctuations available to 99% of molecules at 20–37°C.
source: The finding that values of ΔGscrunch for scrunching and anti-scrunching in TSS selection are ~1 kcal mol−1 bp−1 and ~2 kcal mol−1 bp−1, respectively, implies that TSS selection at positions >2 bp downstream or >1 bp upstream of the modal position would exceed the energy fluctuations available to 99% of molecules at 20–37°C, and therefore explains the observation that TSS selection >2 bp downstream or >1 bp upstream of the modal position occurs rarely (Vvedenskaya et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the energetic data.

claim: TSS selection >2 bp downstream or >1 bp upstream of the modal position occurs rarely.
source: The finding that values of ΔGscrunch for scrunching and anti-scrunching in TSS selection are ~1 kcal mol−1 bp−1 and ~2 kcal mol−1 bp−1, respectively, implies that TSS selection at positions >2 bp downstream or >1 bp upstream of the modal position would exceed the energy fluctuations available to 99% of molecules at 20–37°C, and therefore explains the observation that TSS selection >2 bp downstream or >1 bp upstream of the modal position occurs rarely (Vvedenskaya et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: TSS selection by archaeal RNAP, eukaryotic RNAP I, eukaryotic RNAP II from most species, and eukaryotic RNAP III involves the same range of TSS positions as TSS selection by bacterial RNAP (positions ± 2 bp from the modal TSS).
source: TSS selection by archaeal RNAP, eukaryotic RNAP I, eukaryotic RNAP II from most species, and eukaryotic RNAP III involves the same range of TSS positions as TSS selection by bacterial RNAP (positions ± 2 bp from the modal TSS; Learned and Tjian, 1982; Samuels et al., 1984; Thomm and Wich, 1988; Reiter et al., 1990; Fruscoloni et al., 1995; Zecherle et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: TSS selection by archaeal RNAP, eukaryotic RNAP I, eukaryotic RNAP II from most species, and eukaryotic RNAP III is mediated by scrunching and anti-scrunching driven by energy available in the thermal bath.
source: We propose that TSS selection by all of these enzymes is mediated by scrunching and anti-scrunching driven by energy available in the thermal bath.
evidence: This is a proposal/hypothesis based on the bacterial RNAP findings.

claim: TSS selection by S. cerevisiae RNAP II involves a range of TSS positions of 10 s to 100 s of bp (long-range TSS scanning).
source: In contrast, TSS selection by S. cerevisiae RNAP II involves a range of TSS positions of 10 s to 100 s of bp (long-range TSS scanning; Giardina and Lis, 1993; Kuehner and Brow, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: TSS scanning by S. cerevisiae RNAP II is mediated by scrunching and anti-scrunching involving not only energy from the thermal bath, but also energy from the ATPase activity of RNAP II transcription factor TFIIH.
source: We propose that TSS scanning by S. cerevisiae RNAP II also is mediated by scrunching and anti-scrunching, but, in this case, involves not only energy from the thermal bath, but also energy from the ATPase activity of RNAP II transcription factor TFIIH (Sainsbury et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a proposal/hypothesis based on the bacterial RNAP findings and knowledge of TFIIH.

claim: ATP-dependent, TFIIH-dependent cycles of DNA compaction and de-compaction of 10 s to 100 s of bp have been observed in single-molecule optical-tweezer analyses of TSS scanning by S. cerevisiae RNAP II.
source: This proposal could account for the ATP-dependent, TFIIH-dependent cycles of DNA compaction and de-compaction of 10 s to 100 s of bp observed in single-molecule optical-tweezer analyses of TSS scanning by S. cerevisiae RNAP II (Fazal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The mutationally inactivated RNAP derivative β'D460A lacks a residue required for binding of the RNAP-active-center catalytic metal ion and initiating substrates.
source: In order to assemble, trap, and UV-irradiate RPo in living cells, despite the presence of high concentrations of initiating substrates that rapidly convert RPo into transcribing complexes, we used a mutationally inactivated RNAP derivative, β'D460A, that lacks a residue required for binding of the RNAP-active-center catalytic metal ion and initiating substrates (Zaychikov et al., 1996) (Figure 1—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In vitro, in both the absence and presence of initiating substrates, the mutationally inactivated RNAP derivative remains trapped in RPo, exhibiting the same pattern of leading-edge and trailing-edge crosslinks as for wild-type RNAP in the absence of initiating substrates.
source: Control experiments confirm that, in vitro, in both the absence and presence of initiating substrates, the mutationally inactivated RNAP derivative remains trapped in RPo, exhibiting the same pattern of leading-edge and trailing-edge crosslinks as for wild-type RNAP in the absence of initiating substrates (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Reduction in DNA-fragment length from 2.0 to 1.3 kb enables single-bp resolution in single-molecule DNA-nanomanipulation experiments.
source: To enable single-base-pair resolution, we reduced the DNA-tether length from 2.0 kb to 1.3 kb, thereby reducing noise due to compliance (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; see Revyakin et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Use of 1.3 kb DNA segment provides SEM = 0.5 bp for data subsets of n = 30, sufficient for single-base-pair resolution.
source: Use of 1.3 kb DNA segment provides SEM = 0.5 bp for data subsets of n = 30, sufficient for single-base-pair resolution.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and supported by data.
